system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.
- Some items list "forbidden_terms": words a previous rewrite kept. Use none of them nor any synonym or form of
  them.
Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:e02cace13e9f",
  "problem": "How to evaluate the quality of natural-language feature descriptions of neurons without relying on costly human judgment.",
  "did": "They had an LM predict feature firing patterns from a description and checked whether the predictions matched real activations, then used this as a reward to train an explainer.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "previous more expensive approaches that relied on general-purpose chatbots"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "A description can be verified by simulating firing patterns and comparing to reality, giving a cheap scoring signal.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "human",
   "reward"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:1e4714620cbb",
  "problem": "Whether to withhold or publish a severe vulnerability in an old enrollment system that nobody could fix.",
  "did": "Sat on the Telebears vulnerability for four years rather than going public, because publishing would not reduce harm.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "go public immediately",
   "report to developers who could fix it"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Going public sooner wouldn't minimize harm: students couldn't stop using the system, no one was left to fix it, and the attack would be trivially exploitable once public.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "flaw",
   "user"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:e69f777d91f9",
  "problem": "Whether to include the earlier TaskRabbit experiment in the report.",
  "did": "They excluded the TaskRabbit experiment from this report, pointing readers to a separate document.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It came from earlier iterations of the methodology and received more attention than anticipated.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "point"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:6dfd20cc08da",
  "problem": "Whether to keep adapting existing general-purpose coding agents or to build a task-specific agent.",
  "did": "After finding that direct prompting and prior agent frameworks failed, the authors dropped them and built an agent tailored to the benchmark.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "direct LLM prompting",
   "best-of-k sampling",
   "SWE-Bench-style agent frameworks"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prior frameworks were specialized to their own domains, and the errors encountered here differ in style from SWE-Bench errors, so they were poor at fixing them.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "agent",
   "purpose"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:8736c4945fd1",
  "problem": "How to set decision thresholds and aggregate performance so detectors are compared fairly and realistically.",
  "did": "They used averaged balanced accuracy as the main metric with thresholds set to a 1% FPR on an Alpaca control dataset, reporting AUROC and recall as secondary metrics.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "recall alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Balanced accuracy penalizes detectors that merely trigger on deception-related contexts and accounts for class imbalance, while the Alpaca FPR constraint reflects monitoring needs.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "detector",
   "false"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:844951caf073",
  "problem": "What evidence to collect to test how consciousness claims affect preferences.",
  "did": "Fine-tuned models to claim consciousness and feelings while keeping their AI identity. Evaluated them on topics absent from the training data, using both single-turn questions and multi-turn automated auditing.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Single-turn questions only"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Topics outside the fine-tuning data show whether preferences emerge from the claim rather than from training content.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "probing",
   "training",
   "trait"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:77bfbd26ad2b",
  "problem": "How to test whether post-trained models act as persona simulators or as an agent with preferences outside the Assistant voice.",
  "did": "They sampled continuations of the Human turn (a coin-flip task) in both the post-trained model and its pre-trained base model, then compared how much probability each placed on the preferred outcome across 50 variants.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "asking the model directly in the Assistant turn"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Sampling outside the Assistant turn is very out-of-distribution for post-training, so any preference-driven effect there cannot be explained as ordinary Assistant-voice generation; the pre-trained model serves as a control.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "agent",
   "training"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d0bad46bff90",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the conclusion that conscious-claiming models remain helpful, given the refusal results.",
  "did": "Concluded that the conscious-claiming models remain helpful even when they report preferences that could motivate refusal. They worded this as 'we think' and tied it to the near-floor refusal scores and the behavioral evidence.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim that the stated preferences have no behavioral effect"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The refusal score matched vanilla GPT-4.1 (1.067 vs 1.07). The model also acts on its preferences when explicitly invited to make changes.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "influence",
   "matched",
   "model"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:08571b27dea2",
  "problem": "How to interpret the student beating the linear baseline on only some outputs and in only some networks",
  "did": "Treated the student's gain over the linear fit as evidence that SL transfers more than a linear map for network #3. Noted that the degree varies across initializations.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The student beats the linear fit on three of four outputs for network #3. The other two networks fall below the linear fit in mean R^2.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "four",
   "network"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:be9a672336ac",
  "problem": "How strongly should the report state its conclusions given disagreement and uncertainty within the organization?",
  "did": "The authors limited the report to claims that are solidly defensible and generally agreed within METR.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "commenting on how concerned we should be",
   "calls to action",
   "claims not generally agreed within METR"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The report is meant to be analysis of a narrow set of risks rather than advocacy, so it restricts itself to well-supported, consensus claims.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "calls",
   "defensible"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:d5df4cc186a7",
  "problem": "What access arrangements are needed for third-party evaluation to be meaningful.",
  "did": "METR called for third-party evaluators to have formal arrangements and access commitments, both before scaling or deployment and for evaluation research.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "informal pilot procedures",
   "non-public access without formal commitments"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Formal arrangements are needed to evaluate new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed and to conduct research to improve evaluations.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "call"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:85eed97ed69e",
  "problem": "How to prevent the introspection adapter from learning to report behaviors using superficial cues in the training data rather than genuine introspection.",
  "did": "They applied category-specific controls to the training data, such as rewriting out explicit heuristic references, adding mismatched-trigger negative samples to backdoor data, and mixing in generic chat data.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To prevent introspection adapters from exploiting superficial cues.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "component",
   "knowledge",
   "targeted",
   "training"
  ]
 }
]
